No weights are needed (training is from scratch), the paper's hyperparameters (h=10, bigrams, 5 epochs, lr in {0.05,0.1,0.25,0.5}, 20 CPU threads) are fully specified, no GPU is required, and the host's 22 CPU cores match the paper's 20-thread CPU setup, so training costs seconds-to-minutes. What remains is environment plumbing rather than missing science: the Linux/POSIX build path and the dataset download. Fallback if the native build cannot be made to work on Windows is to install the same code as a prebuilt wheel (pip fasttext-wheel / fasttext) or, worst case, use the authors' own PyTorch EmbeddingBag fastText model (python/doc/examples/FastTextEmbeddingBag.py) as the training engine, with the caveat that the latter is a re-implementation and would downgrade the verdict to partially_reproduced.

approach: The paper's exact system is the authors' own fastText C++ supervised trainer, and the repo ships classification-results.sh which downloads the Zhang et al. 8-dataset release and trains/evaluates every Table 1 row, so the plan is plumbing rather than re-implementation: get a working fasttext engine, get AG News in `__label__N` format, then run the authors' configuration `-dim 10 -wordNgrams 2 -epoch 5 -lr <lr> -thread 20`. A thin reproduce.py drives everything with the Python binding (fasttext-wheel on Windows, native build or `make` when a POSIX toolchain exists), reconstructs the missing validation split (10% of the 120k train set, assumption A4) to pick lr from {0.05, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5}, then retrains on the full training set and evaluates on the official 7.6k test set. The same driver also emits the no-bigram C2 row for free. Only results/metrics.json is written by us; all training/eval numbers come from the authors' binary or its official Python binding, and the fallback to the authors' PyTorch EmbeddingBag example is explicitly flagged as a re-implementation. Everything is CPU-only with 20 threads, matching the paper.

C2 run (cheap): repeat the final training with -wordNgrams 1 at the selected lr and evaluate on data/ag_news.test.

Label vocabulary: sorted label set equals {__label__1,__label__2,__label__3,__label__4}; no row lacks a label prefix.
Feature sanity: report dictionary word count and the fraction of the 10M bin space probed by bigrams (fastText verbose=2 prints these), and confirm minn=maxn=0 so no character n-grams leak in.

Sanity baseline: unigram fastText (wordNgrams=1, 1 epoch, lr=0.1) on the 108k search set should reach roughly 85-90% on the validation set, comfortably above the 25% chance level; if it is near chance the data conversion (labels/tokens) is wrong.

args.summary:
Reproduced claim C1 of "Bag of Tricks for Efficient Text Classification" (arXiv:1607.01759): fastText with h=10 hidden units and bigram features on AG News.

RESULT: C1 test accuracy = 92.04% on the official 7,600-example AG News test set (target 92.5%, absolute tolerance 1.0, |error| = 0.46) -> PASS. The no-bigram row C2 was also produced for free: 91.54% (target 91.5%, |error| = 0.04) -> PASS.

Engine: the authors' own unmodified fastText C++ supervised trainer, used through its official pybind11 binding (prebuilt `fasttext-wheel` 0.9.2, installed via pip; no compiler exists on this Windows host, so the native `make` path was unavailable). No author code was rewritten — `fasttext_engine.train()` forwards its kwargs verbatim to `fasttext.train_supervised` and `test()` calls `model.test(path)`, i.e. the same code path as the authors' `./fasttext supervised` / `./fasttext test`.

Data: AG News from the Zhang et al. (2015) release already present in REPRO_DATA_CACHE (120,000 train / 7,600 test, 4 balanced classes), converted to `__label__N <tokens>` lines with a line-for-line Python port of the authors' own `normalize_text` in repo/classification-results.sh (lowercase, `__label__` prefix, punctuation spacing, quote removal, space squeezing, shuffle). The paper's undisclosed validation split was reconstructed as a 10% holdout (12,000 rows) carved from the 120k train set; the split is duplicate-group-aware (articles are bucketed by normalized text, whole buckets assigned to one side) so no article text appears on both sides — 119,843 duplicate-free groups, verified by assertion.

Protocol: dim=10, wordNgrams=2, epoch=5, thread=20, minCount=1, minn=maxn=0, loss=softmax, bucket=10M, lrUpdateRate=100 (linear decay), lr selected on the validation holdout from {0.05, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5} exactly as Section 3.1 specifies. The search picked lr=0.1 (valid 92.25%); the final model was retrained on the full 120k train set and evaluated on the 7.6k test set. Intermediate checks (row counts, class balance, label set, train/valid disjointness, unigram sanity baseline at 91.9% >> 25% chance) all pass.

Runtime: 43 s end-to-end for the full run (data prep + checks + 4-point lr search + final bigram and unigram models + test), far inside the 20-minute clean re-run limit; verified by deleting data/, models/ and results/ and re-running `python reproduce.py` from scratch. Target values are read from state/claim_contract.json (never typed into the code) and are used only for the reported pass/fail tolerance check, never as an input to training.

Deviations logged in metrics.json: bucket=10M rather than the 100M the paper mentions for the non-bigram-only case (dim=10 x 100M bins would need ~4 GB for the input matrix); the validation split is a reconstruction; fastText's asynchronous multi-thread SGD is inherently nondeterministic, so the selected lr and the exact accuracy vary by a few tenths of a point between runs (both observed runs passed).
